prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of Fancy Truck, a producer of trucks that sells mostly to logistics services companies. Fancy Truck's main current product is a truck called Evolution. Now they came up with a new engine, and they want to start selling another type of truck, called Revolution, that will use this engine. The only difference between Revolution and Evolution is the engine, and Fancy Truck's plan is to have both Evolution and Revolution in the market.
prompt.question: The CEO hired us to help him find out a pricing strategy for Revolution. How would you approach pricing this new truck?

clarifying_info.q: Does anyone else have a similar model on the market?
clarifying_info.a: Nobody has a similar model, so competitor pricing is not applicable.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of fuel?
What is the useful life of the trucks?
clarifying_info.a: Both Evolution and Revolution have a useful life of 4 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the salvage value of each truck?
clarifying_info.a: Salvage value is the same for both trucks.

clarifying_info.q: How many kilometres do clients drive per year on average?
clarifying_info.a: On average, clients drive 250 thousand km per year.

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost Fancy Truck to produce Revolution vs Evolution?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs are the same for both, but Revolution costs $10 thousand more per truck to produce due to the more complex engine.

exhibits.title: Truck Comparison Table
exhibits.shows: Side-by-side specifications of Evolution and Revolution trucks

Revolution.fuel_efficiency: 25% more km with same fuel (i.e. 12.5 km/L)

data.note: Salvage value the same for both; clients drive 250,000 km/year on average

exhibits.title: Market Survey — Demand at Three Price Points
exhibits.shows: Survey results showing the percentage of customers who would buy Revolution vs Evolution at three different Revolution price points

framework: Understand customer value drivers (driver needs, purchaser needs, maintenance needs)
Identify applicable pricing methodologies: competitor-based (N/A here), cost-based, value-based
Quantify value delivered to customer via fuel savings over truck lifetime to set value-based price ceiling
Use market survey data combined with incremental production cost to determine profit-maximising price point
Consider qualitative factors that may limit willingness-to-pay (risk aversion, adoption hesitancy)
Synthesise into a pricing recommendation and next steps

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — What are customers' main considerations when choosing between Evolution and Revolution?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use a clear structure, e.g. Driver Needs (fuel efficiency, reliability, ease of maintenance), Purchaser/Fleet Manager Needs (total cost of ownership, price, financing), and Maintenance Needs (spare part availability, mechanic familiarity, engine complexity). Key answers: price, fuel efficiency, durability, maintenance costs, spare parts availability.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — How would you come up with a price for Revolution?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose at least two or three methods: (1) Competitor benchmarking — not applicable since no similar model exists; (2) Cost-plus — add a mark-up to production cost; (3) Value-based — estimate how much value (fuel savings) Revolution brings to customers over its lifetime and price up to that value. Value-based is the most important method here given the unique engine.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 — Given Evolution sells for $100K, calculate the maximum price Fancy Truck could charge for Revolution on a value-based basis.
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate the lifetime fuel cost difference between the two trucks and add that to the Evolution price. Zero cost of capital may be assumed, but no other simplifications.

math.setup: Evolution fuel cost per year = (250,000 km) / (10 km/L) * $1.50/L. Revolution fuel efficiency = 10 * 1.25 = 12.5 km/L. Revolution fuel cost per year = (250,000 km) / (12.5 km/L) * $1.50/L. Lifetime saving = 4 years * annual difference.

questions.prompt: Phase 4 — Using the market survey and the incremental production cost of $10K, which of the three prices ($100K, $115K, $130K) maximises Fancy Truck's profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate must ask for or note the incremental production cost before calculating profits. The goal is profit maximisation, not revenue maximisation. Compare incremental profit per 100 trucks at each feasible price point. $100K should be immediately dismissed since the extra cost is $10K with zero extra revenue vs Evolution.

math.setup: Extra revenue per Revolution vs Evolution pricing; extra cost = $10K per truck. Evaluate per 100 trucks sold at each price point.
steps: $100K: extra margin per truck = $100K - $100K - $10K = -$10K → worse than Evolution; reject
$115K: extra margin per truck = $115K - $100K - $10K = $5K; 80 Revolution buyers per 100 trucks → incremental profit = 80 * $5K = $400K per 100 trucks
$130K: extra margin per truck = $130K - $100K - $10K = $20K; 40 Revolution buyers per 100 trucks → incremental profit = 40 * $20K = $800K per 100 trucks
$130K generates $800K vs $400K at $115K; market size is not needed to determine the better choice
math.answer: Price Revolution at $130K; incremental profit of $800K per 100 trucks vs $400K at $115K

questions.prompt: Phase 5 — Why would some customers still buy the old Evolution model even if Revolution was priced the same?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm adoption barriers and risk factors unrelated to price.

brainstorming.prompt: Why do you think some customers would still buy Evolution even if Revolution were priced the same?

categories.name: Technology Risk / Trust
ideas: Logistics companies want to test the new truck before committing their entire fleet
Uncertainty about whether the claimed fuel efficiency is achievable in real conditions

categories.name: Maintenance & Spare Parts
ideas: No used/reconditioned Revolution engines available, making third-party repairs harder
Fewer mechanics familiar with the new engine, raising repair costs and downtime risk

categories.name: Operational Disruption
ideas: Fleet operators prefer homogenous fleets for simplified driver training and maintenance scheduling
Switching costs if workshops are tooled only for Evolution engines

categories.name: Financial / Contractual
ideas: Existing fleet replacement contracts or financing tied to Evolution
Budget cycles that make a new (even same-priced) truck a separate approval item

recommendation: Set the Revolution price at $130,000, delivering $800K incremental profit per 100 trucks sold versus $400K at $115K
The $130K price is also the maximum value-based ceiling derived from lifetime fuel savings ($30K over 4 years), ensuring customers still capture value relative to Evolution
risks: Actual customer adoption may be lower than survey suggests if fuel efficiency is not realised in practice
Logistics companies may delay full fleet transition, reducing near-term Revolution volumes
Competitor entry with a similar engine could erode the premium over time
next_steps: Validate fuel efficiency claims through pilot programme with select logistics customers
Develop a fleet transition roadmap and financing options to accelerate adoption
Monitor competitor landscape for similar engine developments
Assess after-sales service readiness — mechanic training and spare parts supply for Revolution engine
